chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Al-Hasan ibn Atiyya, from Umar ibn Yazeed, who said:

I and Umar were in Al-Medina, so Umar sold Harawiyya saddlebags, each bag from it for such and such. So I took it and distributed it, but they found a defect, so they returned it. So Umar said to them, 'I shall give you its price which I sold it with'. They said, 'No, but we shall take from you a price of the cloth'. So Umar mentioned that to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), so he (peace be upon him) said: 'That is binding for him (the buyer)'.

key_terms.جِرَابٌ هَرَوِيٌّ: Harawiyya saddlebag (a type of bag from Herat)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling when a buyer returns a defective good in Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the principle of *Khiyar al-'Ayb* (option of defect) in Shia jurisprudence, where the buyer retains the right to choose between returning the item for a full refund of the price (*thaman*) or keeping it after paying its true value (*qimah*). The Imam’s confirmation that the buyer's choice is binding (*Yalzamuhu thalika*) underscores the contractual autonomy granted to parties in commercial transactions, provided the defect was not known at the time of sale. This ruling highlights the Shia emphasis on fairness and transparency, ensuring that the seller bears the risk of hidden defects while allowing the buyer to mitigate loss without penalty.
